entries.title: Celebrity, sex and motherhood misery: the 10 best books by Rachel Cusk … ranked!
entries.summary: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial authorIn Cusk’s headline-grabbing latest, a writer invents the biography of a film star who sounds very like Natalie Portman. entries.content:
10 Life of M(2026)

In Cusk’s headline-grabbing latest, a writer invents the biography of a film star who sounds very like Natalie Portman. Set in the now standard late-Cusk sans serif typeface (no frivolous flourishes!), Life of M serves up observations on fame in a light fictional coating. “To always be playing a part is to have no home.” Having made her name as a devilishly good creator of brainy social comedies, Cusk’s pivot to wintry autofiction since the Outline trilogy appears to have reached its logical conclusion in this flat, abstracted portrait of empty celebrity. The New York Times called it “rarefied, cosmopolitan, self-serious”.

Sample line: “Everything I did or said in her company was false. It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real.”

9 The Lucky Ones(2003)

A collection of stories about diverse characters who are linked by the influence of a newspaper columnist. They start weakly – Cusk struggles to embody a working-class female prisoner – but improve once she turns her caustic eye to ski trips and lawyers. The short form enables Cusk to show a narrative strength we don’t always see.

Sample line: “Jane and Thomas were ironing out their lives in preparation for parenthood, starching and folding and putting away their youth, their excitement, their spontaneity.”

8 Saving Agnes(1993)

After a cracking first line (“The house, like the party, was subsiding”), Cusk’s cheerfully comic debut tickles the reader throughout, as Agnes Day looks for love in contemporary London. Published to acclaim (and a Whitbread award) when Cusk was 26, it has a young writer’s weakness for using elaborate locutions as a shortcut to comedy, but there’s energy on every page, and her phrasing is always perfect: Agnes’s friend Merlin has “a salary for which Elizabeth Bennet would have left Darcy’s dinner burning in the oven”.

Sample line: “Like a mirror he gave back nothing but what was already there; smash it and he would be gone, leaving her with nothing but a rearranged face and a few years of bad luck.”

7 The Temporary (1995)

Cusk’s sparky second novel is a romantic dramedy. Two Londoners – publishing temp Francine and posh Ralph – bond over a dried-out risotto “like a dish of planetary matter brought back by an alien”. Francine’s house moves frustrate her mother (“You’ve quite ruined my new address book, what with all the crossings-out”); then Ralph wants to move on too. “I thought she understood it was just a temporary thing.” The story builds to an impressively messy climax, with Cusk switching between viewpoints and building tension.

Sample line: “‘I’m something of an intellectual myself,’ Neil had said, straightening a tie across which autonomous golf clubs roamed.”

6 Second Place(2021)

A writer, M, invites the devilish painter L to live in her home, and some chewy stranger-in-our-midst stuff ensues, upending family life and giving the opportunity for some classic Cuskian observations. “I need to get at the truth of a thing and dig and dig until it is dragged painfully to light.” There’s drama – as L humiliates M and her husband – and comedy, as M’s daughter’s boyfriend reads everyone his terrible novel-in-progress. Inspired by DH Lawrence’s stay in New Mexico in the 1920s, Second Place is a curious novel, and it’s the weirdness that makes it interesting.

Sample line: “I’ve been criticised all my life – it’s how I’ve come to know that I’m there.”

5 A Life’s Work(2001)

Cusk’s memoir of “all that love and terror and strangeness” of becoming a mother. It’s a book of scorched-earth candour: Cusk acknowledges her own misery at the drudgery of early motherhood and curses the asininity of childcare books. It was of course controversial, not for its writing – few could fault that – but for daring to challenge a Pollyanna-ish portrayal of parenthood. Cusk was unabashed: “This is not a childcare manual, ladies. In these pages you have to think for yourselves.”

Sample line: “When I found myself pregnant again when Albertine was six months old I greeted my old cell with the cheerless acceptance of the convict intercepted at large.”

4 Arlington Park(2006)

This novel’s Joycean opening settles down to an exquisitely written social comedy. The story of five young mothers, it feels at times like a fictional extension of A Life’s Work: each resents the confinements of motherhood. Perhaps this is what gives the novel its jaundiced eye; not just snobbish (“Mandy Clapp – it was the name on the badge of someone working at a supermarket checkout”) but misanthropic: everyone gets it. “She’d get pretty damned jumpy if her husband’s salary didn’t come rolling in like a Pacific breaker every month, or if people stopped thinking she looked like Felicity Kendal.” But it’s brilliantly funny.

Sample line: “It was funny that she had ended up as a teacher, back at school. It made it seem that she wasn’t bright or gifted or exceptional at all. She was merely good at going to school.”

3 In the Fold(2005)

This novel is a perfect amalgam of the qualities of early Cusk: funny, cynical, rigorous and linguistically precise. Its narrative of characters who are socially and materially conformist but terrified of appearing conventional centres on a man who falls in with a wealthy family. But the upheavals of the plot – things collapse and break – are less important than the sinuous sentences and streams of dialogue. Hidden here, though, we can perhaps see early evidence of Cusk’s desire to break free of conventional fiction. As one character has it: “Better to be broken than to be a slave of method!”

Sample line: “[The schoolboys] make a list of the mothers they’d most like to sleep with. This is the first time she hasn’t made it. It’s so embarrassing for her.”

2 The Country Life(1997)

longest novel is the blackest of all her early comedies, the humour as often situational as verbal. Stella Benson abandons her job and boyfriend to become an au pair for a rural family’s disabled son. She’s not there long before strange, sinister things start to happen. She defaces the gardens by vomiting pink luncheon meat over them. She discovers a book titled The Runaway Bride by Stella Benson. This is a novel of broad and deep character insight, of social awareness – and of unexpected sexual awakening.

Sample line: “I am normally a slow and careful eater, having been schooled by my mother in the many social atrocities it is possible unwittingly to commit during the ingestion of food.”

1 The Outline trilogy(2014-18)

“I had no desire to prove that one book was better than another,” says Faye, the narrator. Well, we do! Outline’s revolution took Cusk’s art to a new place, wholly rejecting traditional character and description, and defining writer Faye – who bears similarities to Cusk – in relation to the people she meets on a trip to Athens. “I was beginning to see my own fears and desires manifested outside myself.” There are stories aplenty, but the overall tone is spare and cool, making something entirely original from the wreckage of Cusk’s need to dispose of her old ways. Two sequels followed – Transit and Kudos – but it was the first book that really shook things up. Critics argued that while it offered “few of the standard expected rewards of fiction”, it was nonetheless “a triumph of attitude and daring”.

Sample line: “But what other people thought was no longer of any help to me. Those thoughts only existed within certain structures, and I had definitively left those structures.”

entries.title: The American Way of Killing by Malcolm Gladwell review – wide of the mark
entries.summary: Gladwell’s highly readable investigation into US gun culture fails to engage with the bigger questionsOnce, while having a steak dinner with Republicans in a small town in Indiana, the man sitting opposite me asked: “How do you cope in London, when Muslims elected that mayor and you have all that gun control?” I’d been in enough such situations to know that there was no “winning” a conversation th
entries.content:
Once, while having a steak dinner with Republicans in a small town in Indiana, the man sitting opposite me asked: “How do you cope in London, when Muslims elected that mayor and you have all that gun control?” I’d been in enough such situations to know that there was no “winning” a conversation that starts like this and so did my best to playfully bat the question away.

“Well, the Muslims didn’t elect a mayor – Londoners elected a Muslim mayor,” I said. “And we don’t talk much about gun control for the same reason we don’t talk about polar bear control: we don’t have many polar bears and we don’t have many guns.”

The quip didn’t land. The table looked at me somewhat bemused. The local party leader leaned over to help dig me out. “They don’t have freedom,” he explained. “They don’t understand freedom.”

In the two decades I spent reporting from America – 12 years as a correspondent for this paper – gun culture was one of two major issues that was difficult to translate (the other was health care). After every high-profile mass shooting, editors in London would ask whether this would finally prompt gun control, while in the US the sale of guns would go up as people “sought protection” from the next shooter.

Malcolm Gladwell’s The American Way of Killing will not help the translation much. Gladwell, who grew up in Canada, sets out to ask why: “a young boy like me can grow up [in one place] without any first-hand experience of lethal violence at all, [while] in another a young man can bury more than a dozen of his closest friends by his 30th birthday … What is so different about the United States?” It’s a big question. And if there’s one thing Gladwell loves, it is big questions.

He is the bestselling author of several popular books including The Tipping Point, which seeks to pinpoint the process by which individual choices turn into social epidemics; Blink, which investigates how we make informed decisions through our unconscious; and Outliers, which seeks to explain success and talent through graft. His method is to blend a breezy, readable writing style with a kind of Socratic, analytical approach that revels in its lack of ideological commitment; exquisite writing and pitch perfect story underpinned by moral ambivalence, which presents its findings as both mould-breaking and iconoclastic.

As social commentary his books are witty, vivid and accessible, providing the kind of nuggets that do well at dinner parties so long as nobody there is remotely impacted by the topic at hand. As meaningful guides to social policy and political intervention they are occasionally insightful but, for the most part, thin and, at their worst, counterproductive. Gladwell’s approach may appear to work when addressing a subject readers have never really thought about, but it breaks down with one – like guns in the US – that has been covered extensively.

Unlike in his previous books, he doesn’t aspire to construct a single argument and then write it through from beginning to end. Instead, he offers a series of discrete, and at times related, observations around America’s relationship to gun violence. His curiosity sprawls across disciplines and themes. He interviews doctors, sociologists, former police chiefs, criminologists, public health specialists, historians, psychologists, legal scholars, and surgeons, while his research takes in supreme court cases, slave history, 17th-century law, physiology, 18th-century grammar and firearms technology.

Evoking the parable of the blind men and the elephant he promises: “chapters on the trunk and the leg and the tusk, and at the end my hope is that by seeing all the parts in one place you will finally get a sense of the whole elephant – and understand that what seems from the outside like an intractable problem need not be intractable at all”.

Many of the chapters make useful corrections to the dominant narrative that are well known but bear repeating. He shows how the drop in gun deaths is due to improvements in surgery and other medical interventions rather than a drop in the number of shootings – showing how America can simultaneously be just as violent but less deadly. He explains how the “militia” mentioned in the second amendment were more about suppressing slave rebellions than defending themselves from state tyranny. He shows that most gun murders are the result of “expressive violence” – impulsive eruptions of anger – rather than “instrumental violence” – conscious, pre-meditated decisions to break the law.

Some are of marginal interest but little real consequence. Following a fairly involved introduction to gun technology he explains why the narrow focus on assault rifles is misguided. He devotes considerable space to litigating case law from 17th-century England which has come up in supreme court trials, as though settling it would in some way settle the legal case around gun control.

A key theme running through the first part of the book is that America’s gun debate (if one can call it that) is undermined by a series of dishonest conversations that disable any substantive conversation. That is true. When Americans think of gun violence they imagine school massacres, gang members and cop shootings. The reality is you are more likely to be shot dead by someone you know than someone you don’t; most people who are killed by guns kill themselves; you are more likely to be shot dead if you have a gun in the house than if you don’t; mass shootings comprise a minority of gun murders; almost twice as many white people are killed by guns than black people; most Americans favour gun control and believe an increase in the number of guns will be bad for the country.

But much of the conversation that Gladwell initiates in the book is not honest either. By avoiding any serious analysis of systemic and structural inequalities – particularly in terms of race and class – he fails to engage with who gets murdered by guns and why. (He alludes to it, obliquely, in a section about how trauma centres are routinely located a significant distance from where black, brown and poor people tend to live, which costs lives.) He talks to doctors on the southside of Chicago, in Baltimore and sociologists in Alabama’s black belt – areas where many black and poor people are shot – without comment as to why that should be.

He advocates for more police, pointing out that the US has fewer police per capita than most European countries (which I certainly would never have guessed), without reflecting on who they tend to shoot and for what reasons. In a nation where non-racial democracy is a relatively new and fragile practice, that could lead to an escalation of violence rather than suppressing it. He derides the slogan to Defund the Police without acknowledging that a central plank of that demand was to shift resources from policing to mental health care, youth work and other social programmes that would address root causes. He deconstructs the confused syntax of the second amendment and concludes that the problem is not that a well-funded lobby, embedded in the far-right, wields disproportionate influence on America’s polity and judiciary, but that “it was written according to a set of rules and grammatical norms that no longer exist”.

As a result the reader is left with a sense that, when it comes to the US and guns, there are various things amiss, but with little idea of how substantial a difference they make to the problem, why they have not been addressed and who suffers as a result. Gladwell manages to skilfully depict the odd trunk, tusk and leg but somehow misses several elephants in the room.

entries.title: The Recovery House by Derek Owusu review – a uniquely honest view of mental health
entries.summary: Writing from firsthand experience, the author offers an affecting meditation on art, mental fragility and faith“What’s in your head?” Dolores O’Riordan’s raw, plaintive refrain loops through the Cranberries’ 1994 hit Zombie. A protest song about the Troubles could, on paper, hardly seem further removed from Derek Owusu’s third novel, about a young writer recovering from a mental health crisis. But
entries.content:
“What’s in your head?” Dolores O’Riordan’s raw, plaintive refrain loops through the Cranberries’ 1994 hit Zombie. A protest song about the Troubles could, on paper, hardly seem further removed from Derek Owusu’s third novel, about a young writer recovering from a mental health crisis. But in an author’s note before The Recovery House begins, Owusu instructs the reader to listen to the song “at least two to four times before going beyond this page”. Gradually it becomes clear that the song’s central question is one Owusu’s protagonist asks in various forms throughout the novel.

Can we ever fully understand what is going on in our own heads? We meet Jamal, a young novelist who has woken up in a recovery house – a residential alternative to hospital admission – after a breakdown. It transpires that he has overdosed, is an alcoholic, and has been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. He is in a frazzled, frantic state, initially less interested in getting better than in piecing together how he got there.

The house itself is hardly a sanctuary in the conventional sense: Jamal finds a single bed with protruding springs, dead cockroaches in the nightstand and restless corridors in which people in various states of distress move around one another. Jamal’s nurses watch him; he watches them back. Owusu knows the world he is writing about – he spent a summer in a recovery house himself after a mental health crisis, and there is an intimacy to the way he renders this suspended, in-between place.

Writing is both Jamal’s vocation and his illness. Like Owusu, he has published two books and won an award for his first; the expectations surrounding the third have become unbearable, and he eventually remembers that it was the attempt to write it that precipitated his breakdown. He comes to the frightening realisation that “the thing that inspired me is the thing that’s trying to kill me”. His frustration with the world of publishing is also evident: “why does everyone in this industry want something from you even though we’re all very aware that things usually take time.”

A woman staying in the room below Jamal sings Zombie’s chorus in the night, over and over, until he finds himself singing it too, flooding his mind in interstitial moments. The singer, Joy, eventually slips a pen and paper beneath his door, something the nurses have refused him for fear of what writing will provoke. From there, they develop a tender, almost soulmate-like friendship, which becomes inflected with religion when the pair begin a weekly Bible study session together. Faith, as rendered by Owusu, is not cruel or exacting. There is something almost prelapsarian in Jamal and Joy’s relationship with God, as there is about their friendship – an innocent, platonic love. Between them, “What’s in your head?” transforms from a fear into an invitation: tell me.

The recovery house gradually becomes a strange, fragile ecosystem for Jamal’s convalescence. He shares cigarettes with its motley crew of residents, observes their dramas and begins to emerge from himself. It offers something a hospital cannot: a temporary, disparate community of people who understand that we are perhaps all closer to the precipice of collapse than we like to imagine. “Who was well in the world anyway?” one of the patients asks, concluding: “there was only the sick and those who didn’t realise it yet”.

At just 160 pages, The Recovery House is a very small book about some very large questions: what separates illness from inspiration? When does that inspiration become compulsion, when does self-examination slip into self-destruction? Owusu is interested in the porous boundaries between these states, and his prose mimics them. Written in long, free-flowing sentences, with sparse punctuation and no conventional chapter markings, the novel has the rhythm of a poem, one thought spilling into the next before it can be contained.

Owusu’s novel is slight enough to cradle in your hands, and it feels as though it must be handled in this way: with care, liable to shatter if held too tightly. It is a uniquely honest and affecting meditation on art, religion and mental health, told with a preternatural tenderness. At times it is almost painfully raw, reading like an excavation of the soul of a writer wondering whether, in turning his life into art, he has also been exploiting it.

entries.title: I was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the Alps
entries.summary: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?When I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come
entries.content:
When I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side.

Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now …

As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else?

Thankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. Perhaps because I’d started with Orient Express, a glamorous setting was a foundational part of the Christie experience for me, especially after I’d watched the 70s film with Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman and Sean Connery sweeping down the platform trailing smoke and old-school Hollywood style. Poirot gets most of the fun, far-flung locations: the French Riviera, Egypt, the Greek islands and the Dolomites, to name a few.

To a younger reader, Miss Marple’s world initially felt quite small in comparison. It was only when I reread the books as an adult that I understood the genius of the character, and came to appreciate how clever and radical Christie had been in making an elderly spinster her master sleuth – occupying a space somewhere between that of a detective and a bystander. She had taken one of the “left behind” women – a figure typically both pitied and scorned by society for not having been able to find a partner after the first world war – and shown her running rings around the other characters, using her invisibility as a kind of superpower. And in creating Miss Marple, she had broken one of the oaths made by the Detection Club (of which Christie was a member) not to use “Feminine Intuition” as a means of solving the crime. So much in the Miss Marple books relies on her intuition: there are physical clues, yes, but it is her understanding of human nature, an understanding that is coded as specifically and peculiarly “female”, that really wins the day.

I came to appreciate Miss Marple’s lack of ego, her sense of humour: she is always in on the joke, always understands and plays up to the image others have of her. I enjoyed her sudden and surprising touches of darkness. I also loved that, while the Poirot books can feel quite timeless, the Marple books form a fascinating portrait of social change in Britain across the decades: the evolving landscape of the English village as documented between the 1930s setting of The Murder at the Vicarage and the 1950s period of The Mirror Crack’d from Side to Side (in which a new housing estate has been built), the postwar unease about not knowing one’s neighbours in A Murder Is Announced and the swinging 60s raciness of At Bertram’s Hotel.

All of which I came to appreciate anew when planning my own novel. I knew that Miss Marple herself was the key to it all, the element I had to get absolutely right. She had to be Christie’s Miss Marple in all her complexity and brilliance. The other vital factor was the perfection of Christie’s plotting: the element that had kept me up into the small hours as a preteen, trying to use all the tools provided to guess whodunnit.

But in other areas I knew that I had to break new ground. I didn’t want this book to be an exercise in ventriloquism – there was only one Agatha Christie, and to try to ape her exactly would be an exercise doomed to failure. It also wouldn’t be any fun, creatively. From the outset I realised that this would be a book in conversation with the original books, and indeed with other Agatha Christie books, but one that delivers new elements, and in doing so has its own raison d’être.

When I learned in my research that Death on the Nile was originally meant to be a Miss Marple novel, I found my jumping-off point: here was my way into the project. A way of including my own love of cinematic locations, and indeed what I had loved about those glamorous Poirot novels, in a new Miss Marple adventure. I would take her on holiday – high in the Swiss Alps, to the Grand Alpine Hotel, with its glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes. I realised, too, that using multiple first-person point-of-view narrators would be a fun way of replicating something Christie does so beautifully: telling us a great deal about her characters by showing how they react to Marple, how they by turns underestimate, admire or fear her.

Finally, I wanted my book to be in conversation with our own times. This wasn’t about shoe-horning in themes, but drawing out parallels between then and now. In doing so I wanted to interrogate modern society’s fear of ageing and the invisibility of old age that has hardly changed since Christie’s time. I wanted to highlight the prevalence of certain toxic male egos at the heart of culture and politics: figures who have attempted, at times, to rewrite history to further their own ends or disappear past misdeeds. All, apparently, with a total lack of consequence.

Which brings me to another thing I love about Christie’s writing: the grim satisfaction of seeing the past catching up with the wicked. The meting out of just deserts. It may not be happening out there in the real world at the moment, but rest assured, it happens here.

entries.title: Is culture alive?
entries.summary: From Mozart to Madonna, dim sum to doughnuts, Shakespeare to Sartre – not all forms of life need DNAOn Mount Athos, in northern Greece, a monk rises before dawn to sing the same office that has been sung on that mountain for more than 1,000 years. He learned it from older monks who came before him, who learned it in turn in an unbroken chain stretching back to Athanasios the Athonite, in AD963.Ove
entries.content:
On Mount Athos, in northern Greece, a monk rises before dawn to sing the same office that has been sung on that mountain for more than 1,000 years. He learned it from older monks who came before him, who learned it in turn in an unbroken chain stretching back to Athanasios the Athonite, in AD963.

Over the centuries, individual monks have come and gone, and yet their chants, prayers, oaths, costumes and ceremonies endure. This persistence is remarkable and revealing: cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally.

I believe that human culture isn’t just an accidental add-on to organic life; rather, it’s a separate expression of life in its own right. But first we should define our terms. What is life? There isn’t just one answer; indeed, the lack of a clear definition has become a kind of bad joke among life scientists, who can’t quite agree what it is they actually study.

One attribute of life that most biologists would say is critical, however, is the encoding, processing and transmission of information. In organic life, this is the function of genes. Information about how to survive and reproduce is written in DNA, processed by cells and transmitted over generations. Thanks to occasional copying errors and the sifting of natural selection, biological information has evolved to produce the extraordinary diversity of life on Earth today.

But millions of years ago, a second kind of self-perpetuating information appeared – one that wasn’t written in DNA or read by cells, but which nonetheless began to replicate and propagate itself through time. And it has evolved and diversified to create the stupefying complexity of the modern world. We call it culture.

Cultures consist of knowledge or behaviours transmitted from one individual to another through social learning. We used to believe culture was uniquely human, but animals have cultures, too. Chimpanzees from some parts of west Africa use rocks to crack nuts, for example, but in other parts they don’t, even though the same nuts and rocks are available; in some places they strip sticks of their leaves to fish termites from their nests; and elsewhere they use moss as a sponge from which to drink water. Each population has its own particular way of doing things.

Our ancestors were apes who presumably had cultures at least as complex as those of chimpanzees. But then, as the Earth moved in and out of a series of ice ages starting about 2.6m years ago, something extraordinary happened. Culture began to overtake genes as the primary force shaping hominin evolution.

We became hunter-gatherers – a lifestyle for which we were ill-equipped genetically, but which nevertheless allowed us to thrive thanks to culture. Cultural innovations accumulated in hunter-gatherer groups – how to knap stone tools, track animals, process a root that would otherwise poison us. Where culture led, genes followed. More sophisticated tools and the control of fire allowed us to prepare and cook food, and consequently our jaws, teeth and guts shrank. At the same time, our brains – organs for acquiring, storing and transmitting cultural information – ballooned.

Bigger brains were not simply a consequence of culture – they accelerated it. As brains became better at learning from others, they could acquire and preserve ever greater amounts of cultural knowledge. But the big breakthrough came with language.

Language is not only a fundamental part of culture; it’s also our most powerful means of transmitting cultural information. Of course, language couldn’t have emerged fully formed. It must have evolved gradually, from a simple form of communication to a more complex one, akin to the languages we speak today.

Once even simple language existed, however, everything changed. Knowledge could be explained. Skills could be taught. Techniques could be learned faster, more accurately and with greater fidelity than mere visual copying could allow. Culture went viral.

As brains became better adapted to a world in which some information was available in linguistic form, and able to learn more words and phrases, language itself became gradually more complex, and capable of transmitting more complex cultural information. This positive feedback between language, culture and our neurological hardware turned the human brain into a sophisticated device for the acquisition and production of language.

Specific words and phrases weren’t hardwired into our brains, of course, but the ability to learn and use them became hardwired. This capability was entirely new, and constituted a crucial turning point in our cultural evolution, as revolutionary and important as the origin of DNA and the genetic code in biological evolution.

Culture and languages diversified wildly as humans spread across the planet, while genetic differences between populations remained minimal. Cultural evolution accelerated away, creating different religions, styles of music, art, farming systems and complex civilisations. It led ultimately to the superabundance of human culture today – from Mozart to Madonna; dim sum to doughnuts; from St Peter’s Basilica to the Taj Mahal; Japanese tea ceremonies to Celebrity Traitors; and from heart transplants to the Hubble space telescope.

Life on Earth has evolved in two phases: first, biological, then cultural. But we may now be on the verge of the next critical juncture in the history of life. We’re currently witnessing the emergence of a new kind of information that can perpetuate itself – machines capable of writing their own code. A third form of life and mode of evolution may be beginning, in which case this will be the most extraordinary moment in human history to be alive as an observer. What might this mean for our future? And what can we learn from the past in order to prepare for this new phase of life on Earth?

Jonathan Loh is an honorary fellow in the School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex, and the author of Life Story: From Cells to Civilisations and Beyond (Bodley Head).

Further reading

Becoming Human: A Theory of Ontogeny by Michael Tomasello (Harvard, £20.95)

The Social Brain: The Psychology of Successful Groups by Tracey Camilleri, Samantha Rockey and Robin Dunbar (Penguin, £11.99)

The Selfish Gene by Richard Dawkins (Oxford, £12.99)

entries.title: Jonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’
entries.summary: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’When HBO dropped its plan to adapt Jonathan Franzen’s bestselling novel The Corrections in 2012, the author was so relieved he says he performed his first and last cartwheel on the lawn of his home in Santa Cruz, California. There had been an attempted film adaptation before
entries.content:
When HBO dropped its plan to adapt Jonathan Franzen’s bestselling novel The Corrections in 2012, the author was so relieved he says he performed his first and last cartwheel on the lawn of his home in Santa Cruz, California. There had been an attempted film adaptation before that, but he had been unsurprised by its failure, having warned that it was impossible to condense his densely plotted doorstopper of a novel into a feature-length film. This time, Franzen had signed up as co-writer, with filmmaker Noah Baumbach. He says that HBO was “excluded from the development process. Mistake, because we didn’t know how to do TV.” Franzen himself hadn’t even owned a telly until a few years earlier and certainly didn’t have cable, so as he was wrestling with the script, he began renting box sets. Around three episodes into one drama series, he realised “we have no idea what we’re doing. This is not how you do TV. This is bad,” he recalls. The result, he says, was “one of the worst pilots anyone has ever made”.

Franzen used to think TV was the “enemy” of the serious novelist. In a well-known 1996 essay for Harper’s Magazine about the decline of high literature he had complained bitterly about the “banal ascendancy of television”. But after the HBO series failed, he watched Breaking Bad, Nurse Jackie and Silicon Valley and loved them. In the age of social media, AI and the endless scroll, TV has started to look like a “friend”, he says now. And The Corrections is finally being adapted into an eight-part Netflix series, with Meryl Streep playing Enid Lambert, the matriarch clinging to dreams of hosting a perfect last family Christmas, even as her husband Alfred is in terminal decline with Parkinson’s and dementia and their grownup children’s lives are falling apart in terrible, comical ways. Once Streep announced she was in, Franzen felt the “chances of making this show have gone up above 50%”. He says he’s a month away from finishing the script.

We are meeting at his home on the edge of Santa Cruz, in his office where the blinds are pulled down low against the bright sunshine. He is 67, tall and slightly stooped, and although his hair has turned white he still looks boyish when he laughs, wide smile and little snub nose, a wicked glint behind his trademark dark-framed spectacles. He has settled into a chair that seems too small for his lanky frame and frequently squirms with discomfort. Should we try switching places, I ask at one point? “No, I’m just physically expressing discomfort with repeating myself,” he replies. He likes to edit his speech as he goes along: “strike that word!” he orders at one point, and “this needs to be underlined”. When he loses his thread he announces, grandly, “you can redirect”.

The Corrections, Franzen’s third novel, won the 2001 National book award for fiction in the US, and remains one of the bestselling works of literary fiction of recent decades. It was published a few days before 9/11 and distils the materialism, anxieties and complacency of America’s long 20th century. It is also Franzen’s most “autobiographical novel”, drawn loosely from his own midwestern upbringing: Franzen was raised in an affluent suburb of St Louis, Missouri. Like Alfred, his dad, who was an engineer, developed Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, while Enid is a “cartoon version” of his own mother. “There are not very many incidents from my life in the book but those two: the personalities and the self-deception about the gravity of the mental deterioration – that’s all drawn from my own experience,” he says.

Franzen says he learned his “psychology as a novelist” from his family. His parents were “powerful characters”: they were “hilarious” and “terrifying” and also “thoughtful”, with rich interior lives. “They created not only Enid and Alfred, but really the notion of a character … the combination of intellectual substance, emotional wanting, emotional needs and comedy,” he explains. His father died before The Corrections was published. His mother lived long enough to know that an extract had appeared in the New Yorker, as part of a special issue dedicated to American writers under 40.

“My annoying aunt, her sister, called her up and said: ‘Irene: do not read Jon’s piece in the New Yorker,’” Franzen recalls. His mother was ill with cancer and had been given months to live. He visited her a few days after that phone call, when inevitably her question was “Why shouldn’t I read your piece in the New Yorker?”. He summarised the story for her, “making some small omissions, but basically just describing what the thing was”. When he was finished, she said: “Thank you, I don’t need to read it.” It was one of their last long conversations. She died 10 days later. “My parents gave us kids everything – including a lot of criticism. But then they just exited, and I was still in my 30s and could write whatever I want,” he says. He could not have published The Corrections had they been alive. Most of his subsequent novels – including Crossroads and Freedom, two other big, ideas-filled books – have also centred on dysfunctional midwestern families. “It always puzzles me that people find it remarkable that I have characters who are related through family in my books,” he says, sounding a bit put out. “Because it’s like, well, the Bible is a book of family stories. The Old Testament, it’s all family stories. The Greek myths, Homer …”

Franzen initially studied science at university: “That was a bit of a beard to get my parents to pay for college,” he says. They were not happy when he switched majors, “but at least I did something serious like German literature as opposed to a frivolous English major, which they literally would not have paid for.” After graduating from Swarthmore, a liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, in 1981, he won a year-long Fulbright scholarship at the Freie Universität in Berlin. His first novel, The Twenty-Seventh City, was published six years later, in 1988. He has worked full-time as a writer ever since. “I made nothing but mistakes as a young person but actually was lucky enough to realise, this is what you’re good at,” he says.

Franzen describes The Corrections as an “angry comedy” and he has a reputation for being, well, an angry guy. Where does his anger come from, I wonder? “It’s still mysterious to me, having so many privileges – not really economic privilege, but every other imaginable kind of privilege – that I was angry for so long. There’s 14 years of being in a marriage that should have ended after two years. That explains a lot, actually,” he says. He married a fellow writer, Valerie Cornell, soon after graduating, and they divorced in 1994. “Then there’s you know, I’m a bright guy, and the stupidity of the world makes me angry.” Oh, and in the 90s, he spent a lot of time “angry that people were seen to be losing interest in the kind of novels that I wrote”. But, he adds, “I don’t know why people think of me as angry now, because I haven’t really been angry in that way since a year after The Corrections was published.”

That first year, he concedes with a wry smile, was a little “bumpy”. Many will remember his spat with Oprah Winfrey, who picked The Corrections for her book club and invited him on to her show, only to rescind her invitation after he described her other picks as “schmaltzy”. The pair later made up – she picked Freedom for her book club in 2010, and they hugged on live TV. One of his problems, he points out, is that he cannot “start a thought without injecting a counterthought to it”. Read only half the quote and he comes across like an “asshole”. While criticising her picks, he also praised Oprah for promoting reading, for instance. He can see now that she was right to be annoyed. But, counterthought: “Well, some of her earlier picks were …” theatrical pause “… schmaltzy.”

Other spats have followed, with the writer Jennifer Weiner over the disproportionate attention given to Franzen’s work. Thought: Weiner is “freeloading” on the gender debate and “asking for a respect that not just male reviewers, but female reviewers, don’t think her work merits”. Counterthought: the gender bias in literature is a genuine problem. He got into trouble for saying he considered adopting an Iraqi orphan to better understand young people. Counterthought: that mad idea lasted six weeks at the most. Franzen says he has learned to become more circumspect. “I didn’t know what I was doing. I didn’t know how to talk to people in an interview. I didn’t know how to do TV. I would just say whatever I was thinking about and then I would get into trouble and I would feel like: ‘Oh, unfair! I’m getting into trouble.’ Well, you know, dude, wise up, learn how to protect yourself. Don’t say those things.”

In 2010, following the publication of Freedom, Franzen appeared on the cover of Time magazine, a rare achievement for any writer. The piece described him as the “Great American Novelist”. He says it was his suggestion that he should be the cover. He got his publicist to contact Time to say they hadn’t had a writer as a cover star for ages, and Franzen would be great. Wait, what, I ask, shuffling through my notes, doesn’t that piece describe you as “singularly ungifted at what you might call brand management”? “Isn’t that hilarious?” he asks, his eyes widening in delight. “It’s hilarious!”

He doesn’t think much of the phrase “great American novel”, though. “It’s usually not said kindly. It’s sort of mocking,” he says. He puts on a bullying sneer: “Oh, the great American novelist. Oh, you’re going to write the great American novel, are you?”

Franzen is not as down on the future of the literary novel as he used to be. That Harper’s essay? His real complaint at the time was “people weren’t buying books like mine”, he says, pretending to sob. “Actually, they were. They were just not buying my novels. That was my complaint in the 90s, and of course I blew that up into some huge cultural problem.” These days, he thinks those who bemoan the decline of reading need some perspective. “I think the doom-criers about the novel tend to make a fundamental mistake. They imagine some golden age when everyone read Flaubert. There was never a time,” he says. It’s true, he continues, that modern technology does little to help cultivate a love of reading. “It’s easy to imagine a time soon when there is no reason to be able to read, because text can be converted into spoken language and you don’t have to write because you just speak and it can be written for you,” he says. But that hardly feels like the worst thing happening in the world right now. “That’s the other thing I feel about the doom-criers of the novel, it’s like, really, this is a world historical problem? People can’t read Steinbeck any more? It’s sad, but nothing lasts for ever. What do you want?”

Franzen says he doesn’t want to comment on American politics because “nobody cares what the novelist thinks”, plus he did an interview with the German newspaper Die Welt before Donald Trump’s second term in which, like many pundits, he predicted that the president wouldn’t follow through on most of his promises and “it’s like no, I was all wrong”. He was, however, on to Trump early. He wrote about the future president in his 1992 novel, Strong Motion, and in various essays that decade. “He symbolised a certain kind of horribleness, a crass, narcissistic, bullying side of American life that, yeah, I noticed early and I hated. I didn’t even live in New York when I wrote Strong Motion and I could feel that odious presence,” he says.

He’s more open to weighing in on environmental issues, having written several feather-ruffling essays for the New Yorker on the climate crisis. He angered climate crisis activists by arguing that humankind needs to accept that global warming is going to happen and start refocusing on local projects devoted to conservation and biodiversity. A passionate birder himself, in 2015 he criticised the bird conservation organisation Audubon for falsely claiming that climate change is the main threat faced by birds, rather than collisions with glass windows and hunting by cats, two more fixable problems. Audubon responded by accusing him of “extreme intellectual dishonesty”. “They’ve apologised,” he says when I ask him about it, “full stop.”

Franzen discovered his passion for birds soon after The Corrections was published. He goes on birding trips whenever he can, but he can also spot a lot from his home: there are violet-green swallows nesting next door, and hooded orioles in the back garden. If it wasn’t so hot, and his blinds weren’t drawn so low, we’d probably see a family of quail running past his office window. “If you want to see quail, this is one of the best places in the world,” he says.

He shares his home with his longtime partner, the writer Kathryn Chetkovich. In a corner of his office there is an electric guitar. He picked up the guitar while working on Freedom, and has this morning been practising with the band, Shady Characters, which he formed with Chetkovich’s brothers. It’s a purely private hobby. “I have never performed in public, and I never will,” he announces.

Last June, Franzen published a new story in the New Yorker about an aspiring teenage actor suffering an unwanted pregnancy and a crisis of faith. It will form part of his next novel, a sequel to Crossroads, which was published in 2021 as the first book in a proposed trilogy. Does that mean his next book is imminent? “This is not, ‘I’ve delivered the manuscript and we’re getting a little teaser.’ No, this is a ‘I’ve gone deep into the cave and I need to send a sign of life,’” he says. It takes Franzen many years to write a novel, and the years before he has settled on a new project are often “horrible”, he says. He tries to distract himself, often by writing nonfiction, and then “I periodically go back and beat my head against the proverbial brick wall”. “It’s not fun,” he confirms: “Some other day, another idea. Yeah, that one didn’t work either. Wake up in the middle of the night. Yeah, I got it. No, you don’t.”

Franzen believes the most difficult part of writing a new novel is that it requires him to change: he needs to become “the kind of person who can write the novel. I’ve had to become a different person in some significant way to get each book written.” To move from The Corrections to Freedom he had to let go of his anger. To write Crossroads, he had to become more forgiving. Right now, he says, “I’m waiting to wake up as the person who is alive again and not the same person he was five years ago.”

Does this mean he sees writing as a means of self-improvement? God, no! When he’s working on a scene, trying to capture a character or get the tone right, he’s not thinking in moral terms. “If you’re really engaged with that, it’s not a matter of morality, but a matter of getting at something true. So I prefer truth as a goal to morality, to self-improvement, to the betterment of one’s soul,” he says. “I don’t really care about bettering my soul. I care about getting it right,” he adds. And then, the reflexive edit: “Which is a pretty good ending line.”

entries.title: The best books to read in September: new paperbacks from Margaret Atwood, Kiran Desai and Richard Holmes
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some great new paperbacks, from an epic multigenerational saga by a Booker winner to a biography of an iconic Victorian poet*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny

Kiran Desai

This Booker-shortlisted novel is about work as much as it is about the relationship between Sunny Bhatia and Sonia Shah, whose families are neighbours and whose attempts to make a match begin their on-off liaison. Where Sunny dreams of journalistic success, Sonia’s heart and mind lie in writing fiction. The dilemma facing an Indian writer, she ponders, is one of obeisance to the west’s appetites and projections.

Desai’s solution to the problem in this immensely entertaining and generative novel is to dart continually between modes of representation and register. The gothic novel appears with the early introduction of the monstrous Ilan de Toorjen Foss, a narcissistic artist who seduces Sonia, suppresses her literary endeavours and then abandons her. The predicaments and predilections of Sunny and Sonia’s Allahabad relatives create a low-key bourgeois comedy: stranded single aunts, genteel impoverishment, the wrangle over a cook famed for his kebabs.

Capacious and shape-shifting though the novel is, filled with subtexts and shadow narratives, it is still a challenge to hold the contradictions and demands of multiple identities. Desai pictures Sonia and her father listening to the Pakistani singer Iqbal Bano, and reflecting on what the music conjures in them: “To be a citizen of a troubled postcolonial nation gave a person gravitas. To be holding out against the crass new world gave a man gravitas. To be wounded yet fighting on against the barbarians gave one gravitas. To be exiled, abandoned by love and luck, gave them gravitas. What happened within a family, what happened between a couple, was no different from that which happened in a nation under dictatorship, running on fear.”

Whether or not a novel can accurately and productively capture this yearning for gravitas, or the continuum between the personal and the political, is one of the questions posed by The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny. Another is the sheer exhaustion – mental, physical and artistic – caused by the constant need for self-invention and reinvention, whether individual, societal, national or global; and how the form of the novel, created in the European consciousness, can complexify itself to take account of an accelerated, fractured modernity. Desai’s answer to these questions is to make her story both dizzyingly vast and insistently miniature; to make us feel that there is as much at stake in the lives of Vini-Puri, a pair of servant girls not even accorded single-name recognition, as in the grand ambitions of the novel’s title characters. She pulls it off, not only in her manoeuvring of cast and incident, but in her ability to elicit apprehension, laughter, compassion and curiosity in the reader. Alex Clark

£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

We Love You, Bunny

Mona Awad

We Love You, Bunny, is the much-anticipated sequel to Mona Awad’s beloved campus horror/satire of 2019, Bunny. Both books are set at an Ivy League university in a crime-ridden New England town; from various well-seeded clues, we can identify this as Brown University. Here it is called Warren, because the Bunnyverse is unabashedly silly and self-referential. Rabbit jokes abound.

The first book followed Samantha, an alienated, cash-strapped creative writing student cold-shouldered by her workshop cohort, a cabal of four ultra-feminine rich girls who all call each other Bunny. The Bunnies wear fluffy dresses, eat mini food and – as Samantha learns when she’s finally inducted into their cult – express their creativity through demonic rites that involve exploding rabbits. Samantha has to transcend them to find her voice as an artist. The story of Bunny is the result.

We Love You, Bunny begins with Samantha bound and gagged in an attic. The Bunnies surround her, congratulating her venomously on the success of her book. Now they want to tell their story. Passing an axe like a talking stick, they introduce us to four versions of their Bunny-centric world. Then they pass the mic to a special guest.

This follow-up has the key strengths of the original, particularly its scabrous satire on upper-middle-class American femininity. However, it suffers from a certain sequelitis. It’s baggier than the original. Its metaphors for creativity feel less earned. The game of visiting each Bunny’s point of view also disappoints. This is redeemed, however, when we come to the last voice of the novel.

Toward the end, a writing professor passes judgment on the story we’re in: “A touch too camp. Zany. A sort of zany romantasy, isn’t it?” Yes, it is, but Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, and nothing can really be too camp. And if We Love You, Bunny has weaknesses endemic to sequels, it also has their strengths. There’s the fun of meeting the old characters and seeing areas we wondered about before, but it also builds on the original, opening up new territory and making new jokes. And though it’s better to start with the first novel, We Love You, Bunny can be read alone. It’s a goofy, overblown flower of a book with lots of thorns that pleasurably scratch. Sandra Newman

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Buckeye

Patrick Ryan

Opening in the first decades of the 20th century, this luminous and tender novel follows the interwoven lives of two married couples in the fictional town of Bonhomie, Ohio. One half of the first of these couples is Cal Jenkins, the sweet-tempered son of a traumatised first world war veteran, born in the spring of 1920 with (to use the parlance of the era) a mild deformity: “The day you were born and one of your legs came up short,” his father, Everett, tells him, “right then I thought, well, that’s it. If we get into another big one, he’ll never be in it.” The delights of prolepsis!

The US gets into another big one in quite short order, of course. Cal, just as his father predicted, is turned away from the recruitment office and ends up spending his days in drudgery at the local concrete factory instead. A chance meeting with Becky Hanover, a young woman with a dark bob and a loveably whimsical way about her, sees Cal married by the end of the first chapter.

On 8 May 1945, Cal is working a shift at the hardware store owned by Becky’s father when a gorgeous, confused redhead stumbles in. Together, they listen to President Truman announce allied victory in Europe over the wireless – and then she kisses him. The gorgeous, confused redhead is Margaret Salt. Her own equally gorgeous and strangely aloof husband is away on a cargo ship in the Pacific. From here, the novel takes off at full thrust, and, as one of Ryan’s characters summarises it: “people get laid, babies get made, everybody lies to their kids”.

It is no surprise that Ryan cut his teeth writing short fiction: Buckeye is elevated throughout by the precision with which he captures the tiny, haunting glories of everyday suburban life. And for all its quotidian charm, a deep melancholy prevents Buckeye from ever tipping into saccharine nostalgia. Ryan strips away the Bakelite glaze of the American dream to expose the raw flesh beneath. AK Blakemore

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The Wax Child

Olga Ravn

On 26 June 1621, in Copenhagen, a woman was beheaded – which was unusual, but only in the manner of her death. According to one historian, during the years 1617 to 1625, in Denmark a “witch” was burned every five days. The first time this happens in Danish author Olga Ravn’s fourth novel, the condemned woman is “tied to the ladder, and the ladder pushed into the bonfire”. Her daughter watches as she falls, her eye “so strangely orange from within. And then in the heat it explodes.”

The child is watched, in turn, by a wax doll who sees everything: everything in this scene, and everything everywhere, through all space and all the time since it was fashioned. On a basic level, the wax child is a useful narrative device. But it also complicates everything. The temptation, from the distance of the 21st century, is to assume charges against so-called witches to be baseless. But in this case, a well-known one in Denmark, the charges included the making of wax children – and Ravn begins with Christenze Krukow, a real Danish noblewoman who was accused of witchcraft three times during her lifetime, making this wax baby.

Ravn began as a poet, and even in English this lineage is clear. Her work asserts that knowledge inheres in objects, comprehension through smell and taste and blood and guts; through metaphor. “How do I know this?” demands the wax child, at one point. “It is like a gash in me to know it.”

At its best The Wax Child is richly evocative, beautiful, creepy and visceral. “It is the darkest of times, December. From the curvature of the earth, minutes run like droplets from the day.” At other times, there’s a bit too much research just out of sight; the novel can feel elliptical, even baffling. One misses the space, the clarity and freedom of Ravn’s International Booker-shortlisted novel The Employees. But maybe that’s the thing about weaving spells. About poetry, too: demand it makes neat sense, and you begin to have too much in common with the witch-hunters. Aida Edemariam

£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

King Sorrow

Joe Hill

Six oddball but doughty kids fall into the path of a vast and terrible supernatural evil which has come into our world from the outer limits of darkness. They must spend their lifetimes battling it, facing horror after horror in the process.

This is the plot, roughly, of Stephen King’s novel It (his best; no arguments). It is also the plot, roughly, of King’s son Joe Hill’s new horror doorstopper, in which six friends summon the ancient, infinitely malicious dragon King Sorrow from the Long Dark to help them defeat some baddies. Needless to say, their supernatural ritual backfires.

Joseph Hillström King started his career making great efforts to avoid any connection with his famous father, publishing under the pen name he still uses today and avoiding meeting his agent in person (he bears a striking resemblance to his dad). But in this latest novel, he leans into it. There are lines that deliberately echo some of King’s most famous (“The man in black fled across the desert …”); a moment that brings to mind a King plot point (a riddling contest). In this whopper of a novel, Hill is delighting in his family connection, and we delight along with him. King Sorrow is huge, sprawling – and absolutely fantastic. Alison Flood

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

Book of Lives

Margaret Atwood

Book of Lives is less a memoir than an autobiography, not a slice of life but the whole works, 85 years. Where most such backward looks are cosily triumphalist or anxiously self-justifying, hers is sharp, funny and engaging, a book you can warm to even if you’re not fully au fait (and few people are) with her astonishing output, which in the “also by” contents list here fills two pages.

At the co-ed high school Atwood opted for, she soon graduated to the “brain class”. A small, “flat-chested weirdo”, with horn-rimmed glasses, a snaggle tooth, frizzy hair, astigmatism and anaemia, she put her energies into sewing and fancy dress. By 14 she was dating: older, artsy boyfriends “somehow just appeared, like mushrooms after rain”. Poetry pursued her, too: her adolescent efforts were “heavily sensational, sometimes macabre”. According to her school yearbook, her “not-so-secret ambition is to write THE Canadian novel”. But her first publications were poems that appeared under the name ME Atwood, “so I wouldn’t be tagged as a girl”.

From university in Toronto, she moved on to Harvard, a tweedily unglamorous scholarship girl. There she researched the Salem witch trials, which along with the patriarchal norms of Harvard graduate school fed into The Handmaid’s Tale many years later. She wasn’t an active feminist in her 20s, when the idea that “domestic tasks might be shared equally” hadn’t arrived. But the oppression of women increasingly troubled her. And by the time the TV version was made, in the era of Trumpism, it was more salient than ever.

At a party in 1969 she met Graeme Gibson, novelist, trickster, spendthrift, high-energy oddball. He was wearing blue denims, she a “white crocheted lace mini dress with wooden buttons down” (Atwood is scrupulous in recording her changing outfits and hairstyles), and at first she had no awareness of his “non-platonic interest” in her. There were complications: she’d married an American poet, less from love than to spare him being drafted to Vietnam, and Graeme had a child by a woman with whom he had an open marriage, Shirley. A cautious courtship followed; Graeme wooed Atwood with yearning letters. If she’d not met him she’d still have been a great novelist, he said, but she’d have had a lot less fun.

His decline, dementia and death bring a sombre tone to the book’s last pages. Ever the workaholic Ms Fixit, Atwood keeps going rather than miss out on the publicity whirl for The Testaments (her sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale): “Ask yourself, Dear Reader: The busy schedule or the empty chair? I chose the busy schedule. The empty chair would be there when I got home.” She has a pacemaker these days and eventually her body “will decide to go off on an adventure of its own”. But for now mind and body are still together and so, in friendly opposition, are the many selves she unveils here in a “blizzard” of memories and photos: nerdy brainiac, waifish poet, Medusa-eyed feminist, uncanny prophet and one of the great novelists of our time. Blake Morrison

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

History

History

Indignity

Lea Ypi

It starts with a photo. A black-and-white image of a couple relaxing on a pair of sun loungers in front of a luxury ski hotel: him, squinting against the sun; her, smiling at the camera, wrapped in a white fur coat. It is their honeymoon in Cortina, up in the Italian Alps.

The year is 1941, and the woman is Lea Ypi’s grandmother. Ypi saw the picture after it had been posted online by a stranger, gone viral across Albania, and attracted a stream of abuse. “Morally degenerate” was one comment. “Fascist collaborator” another.

And so, in Indignity, Ypi sets off to find out exactly who her grandmother was. It is, she writes, partly out of a sense of duty, to defend her family member from the trolls – a kind of 21st-century version of EP Thompson’s famous call for history to rescue the dead from “the enormous condescension of posterity”. But partly, Ypi admits, it is because she finds the photo unsettling. How to reconcile her beloved, compassionate grandmother with this glamorous young woman living it up in Mussolini’s Italy?

From here, two parallel stories unfold. The core of Indignity is a richly reimagined retelling of Ypi’s grandmother’s life. Born in Salonica (now Thessaloniki) in 1918, Leman Leskoviku came into a world that was already falling apart. Cosmopolitan empires were collapsing into nation states, unsure how to treat families like hers: Albanian-speaking, living in Greece, with a proud record of service to the Ottoman state. Leman’s childhood is shaped by the uncertainty of those years: the trauma of wars just ended, economic decline, and blunt, brutal social engineering. As Ypi describes, millions were forcibly moved across newly drawn borders. Leman’s nanny, one of Salonica’s many Muslim Turks, is barely able to hold back tears as she is packed off to central Anatolia.

Amid the ambiguity, and to escape an unwanted suitor, Leman sets her own life on a different path. At just 18, she decides to move to Albania alone. Ypi’s Ondaatje prize-winning memoir, Free, was haunted by stories of Albanians fleeing to neighbouring countries to escape the violence of the 1990s. This story hinges on a young woman’s extraordinary choice to move the other way. Sami Kent

£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Politics

Politics

One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This

Omar El Akkad

Palestine has many eloquent defenders, and El Akkad is one of them. Born in Egypt, raised in Qatar and Canada, and now a US citizen, he has reported from the Middle East, Afghanistan and Guantánamo. His new book is a response to events in Gaza after 7 October 2023. It is his voice, his bafflement, spilling out after decades of having to keep quiet for the sake of journalistic neutrality or artistic show-don’t-tell, of having to bite his tongue after readers responded to his journalism with racist doubt: “I don’t trust any story about terrorism written by a guy named Omar”.

He turns his back on these old strictures and tells the world what’s wrong as himself, not just reporting but processing all that he has seen and heard. “This is an account of a fracture,” he writes, “a breaking away from the notion that the polite, western liberal ever stood for anything at all.” It is a deft, broken-hearted, rhetorical savaging of comfortable people who say nothing (or pay lip service) but care only about preserving normality, convincing themselves that these things only happen “to certain places, to certain people”.

One Day is passionate, poetic and sickening. It is full of well-earned rage, frustration with those who need this morality to be spelled out. For me it was cathartic, almost spiritual, to have these ugly truths articulated. It stoked and tempered the fires of my own rage. It is an important book, a must-read, if only for the reminder that history always comes down to one simple question: “When it mattered, who sided with justice and who sided with power?” Dina Nayeri

Biography

Biography

The Boundless Deep

Richard Holmes

Alfred Tennyson was a divided soul. He even wrote a poem called The Two Voices in which dual versions of himself argued out the pros and cons of suicide. In this illuminating book, Richard Holmes has chosen to focus on the lesser known of the poet’s personae.

The Boundless Deep is not about the bestselling author of the nation’s favourite poem – The Charge of the Light Brigade – or the laureate lord, pacing along the clifftops of the Isle of Wight or posing for Julia Margaret Cameron’s famous photograph (known derisorily in his family as “the dirty monk”). Instead, Holmes gives us “young Tennyson”, the wildly talented youth whose story is far more rich and strange than that of the bearded celebrity.

The Tennysons, wrote Alfred, were a “black-blooded race”, meaning prone to moods and melancholy. His father, a reluctant clergyman, was angry and very often drunk. There was an incident, the details of which are obscure, that resulted in the family cook being burned to death in the rectory kitchen. One of Alfred’s brothers was confined to a lunatic asylum as a boy and stayed there for life. Another suffered from profound depression and followed his father into alcoholism. A third became addicted to opium. Alfred himself suffered from episodes of paralysing gloom and what he called “weird seizures”. His Maud is narrated by a madman: he must often have wondered whether he was or would become one himself.

Holmes is not an uncritical fan – he is tart about the pseudo-medieval flim-flam of Idylls of the King – but when he loves a poem, he writes about it with a wonderful capacity for noticing every pulse of metre, every flicker of nuance. This biography is a compelling story of an odd, brilliant, charismatic character, and a reappraisal of a man who had become so very established we could no longer see him. In giving us young Tennyson – gauche, beautiful, veiled in stinking tobacco smoke – Holmes has given the great poet back to us. Lucy Hughes-Hallett

Biography

Crick

Matthew Cobb

Most people could tell you that Francis Crick, together with James Watson, discovered the double helix structure of DNA, and shaped our understanding of how genes work. Fewer know that Crick also played a key role in modern neuroscience and inspired our continuing efforts to understand the biological basis of consciousness.

Crick once said the two questions that interested him most were “the borderline between the living and the non-living, and the workings of the brain”, questions that were usually discussed in religious or mystical terms but that he believed could be answered by science. In his new biography of the Nobel prize-winning scientist, Matthew Cobb, emeritus professor of zoology at the University of Manchester, does an admirable job of capturing the rare thinker who not only set himself such ambitious goals but made remarkable progress in achieving them, radically remaking two scientific disciplines in the process.

Far from being the stereotypical reclusive genius, labouring in isolation, Crick was loud-talking and charismatic, a philanderer, poetry lover and thrower of risque parties. Crick’s inspiration and breakthroughs came through intense encounters with others, and he was skilled at bringing researchers from different disciplines together to solve scientific puzzles.

In Cobb’s telling, Crick was bold and arrogant, with an uncanny ability to uncover connections and to identify new theoretical and experimental approaches, often challenging far more established experts. Lawrence Bragg, the head of the Cavendish lab, is said to have described him as “the sort of chap who was always doing someone else’s crossword”. This approach meant he often stepped on people’s toes and was occasionally wildly off mark.

Cobb sets himself an ambitious task in trying to do justice to both Crick’s prolific scientific career and his colourful personal life, and this biography is an impressive work of research and scholarship. It is intended to be accessible to the general reader, with the advice that those who are struggling with the science should “follow Crick’s advice to readers of his own books and skip the hard bits”. This general reader struggled often with the technical detail and vocabulary. Some difficulty may be inescapable simply because the science is complex. Nonetheless, it is a relief whenever Crick is quoted, describing his research in his own words, because he had a knack for translating hard science into lay terms. Sophie McBain

Technology

Technology

If Anyone Builds it, Everyone Dies

Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares

What if I told you I could stop you worrying about climate change, and all you had to do was read one book? Great, you’d say, until I mentioned that the reason you’d stop worrying was because the book says our species only has a few years before it’s wiped out by superintelligent AI anyway.

We don’t know what form this extinction will take exactly – perhaps an energy-hungry AI will let the millions of fusion power stations it has built run hot, boiling the oceans. Maybe it will want to reconfigure the atoms in our bodies into something more useful. There are many possibilities, almost all of them bad, say Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares in If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, and who knows which will come true. But just as you can predict that an ice cube dropped into hot water will melt without knowing where any of its individual molecules will end up, you can be sure an AI that’s smarter than a human being will kill us all, somehow.

Yudkowsky and Soares present their case with such conviction that it’s easy to emerge from this book ready to cancel your pension contributions. The glimmer of hope they offer – and it’s low wattage – is that doom can be averted if the entire world agrees to shut down advanced AI development as soon as possible. Given the commercial and strategic incentives, and the current state of political leadership, this seems a little unlikely.

There are certainly moments in the book when the confidence with which an argument is presented outstrips its strength. And Yudkowsky and Soares exhibit more than a touch of confirmation bias. “History,” they write, “is full of … examples of catastrophic risk being minimised and ignored,” from leaded petrol to Chornobyl. But what about predictions of catastrophic risk being proved wrong? History is full of those, too, from Malthus’s population apocalypse to Y2K. Yudkowsky himself once claimed that nanotechnology would destroy humanity “no later than 2010”.

The problem is that you can be overconfident, inconsistent, a serial doom-monger, and still be right. It’s important to be aware of our own motivated reasoning when considering the arguments presented here; we have every incentive to disbelieve them. It still feels like everyone with an interest in the future has a duty to read what Yudkowsky and Soares have to say. David Shariatmadari

Music

Music

Night People

Mark Ronson

Night People is intended as Ronson’s memoir but is as much an attempt to immortalise the people and scenes he came up in as it is a reflection on a childhood shaped by the late-night parties hosted by his parents – first in London, where a distant memory of Robin Williams tucking him in to bed with “Nanu nanu” floats through, then later in Manhattan, when his mother marries Mick Jones from Foreigner.

By his own, self-aware account, Ronson has led a gilded life. Elite schools (Collegiate, Vassar, NYU); sleepovers with Sean Lennon and a cast of New York’s nepo who’s who; hanging out with Michael Jackson; the abundant creative freedom gifted by the safety net of generational wealth. It would be enough to make many readers roll their eyes before turning a single page. Their loss.

Ronson’s talent as a writer enables him to render this privilege, the background glamour, his awkward stumbles as well as successes, with a kind of wry, soft self-deprecation that is genuinely endearing. It helps, of course, that he is a massive nerd. Ronson would rather spend paragraphs enthusing about the thickness of slipmats required for a specific DJ setup than he would recalling the wild-eyed buzz generated at an afterparty close to dawn. On balance, this is a good thing. There is more than enough bad writing on hedonism in the world. I’ll take the earnest, qualitative review of turntable cartridges.

The one-man hit factory, the force who famously drove Amy Winehouse to create her best work, the mega producer – none of that is here, of course. At the centre of this book is a Ronson much closer to the teenage crate-digger whose mum bought him his first Technics turntables and who blagged his way to the booth. It shouldn’t be as compelling as it is, but for the accompanying soundtrack of deep cuts alone, Night People is well worth a spin. Nosheen Iqbal
